schools.summary: Gill reads the Hebrew idiom of lifting up the feet as a mark of cheerfulness rather than of walking, the promises at Bethel having gladdened Jacob, and reports the Jewish saying that his heart lifted his legs so that he walked apace. Calvin finds in the same words the extraordinary strength of his faith, in setting out for a land he did not know, and says of the meeting that followed that Jacob did not fall in with those shepherds accidentally but was guided by a hidden hand, the men who could direct him being brought there at the same hour — so that whenever we wander through intricate windings we should look with the eyes of faith at the secret providence that leads us to unexpected results.

Henry marks what the narrative withholds: every stage of Israel's later march is recorded, but no journal of Jacob's expedition past Bethel, since he had no more such nights and no more such visions, that one being meant for a feast and not for daily bread. He notes the manner of the going and of the arrival — Jacob unburdened by cares, and providence bringing him to the very field where his uncle's flocks were watered — and takes from it his standing lesson, that God is to be acknowledged in the small circumstances that make an undertaking successful, so that timely help is neither chance nor fortune but providence. The rest of his comment runs ahead into the scene at the well: the shepherds' care of their sheep illustrating the concern of the great Shepherd for his flock; the stone explained three ways, as securing scarce water, as sheltering the well, or as keeping the lambs from drowning; the shepherds' watering together showing that separate interests should not keep men from joint help; and Jacob's calling strangers brethren showing both that we should speak civilly and that a man upon his preferment was not ashamed of his trade.

Clarke calls the original very remarkable and hears the same cheerfulness in it, Jacob having seen that with God for his protector he had nothing to fear; he adds that kedem, easterns, covers in the sacred writers all Mesopotamia and the country beyond the Euphrates.

Ellicott glosses the phrase as hastening forward, and draws the picture out: confirmed in the birthright by God as well as man, and promised the divine presence and a safe return, Jacob casts no wistful glances back but travels under the inspiriting influence of hope. He takes the people of the east here for the tribes of northern Mesopotamia rather than the Arabians the phrase usually means.

2.pericope_label: The well in the field and the stone upon it

schools.summary: Gill supposes the well was sought and not stumbled on — Jacob knowing that households and shepherds water there and that he could ask after Laban, or else looking for the particular well where his grandfather's servant had met Rebekah — and passes on two travellers' claims, a fountain at Orpha which Jews, Armenians and Turks alike called Jacob's well, and a fine well near Alexandretta not far from what the Greeks show as the ruins of Laban's house.

Clarke notes that the word for the flocks means small cattle, that sheep in cold countries seldom drink though the practice was probably different in a hot one, and that the three flocks already at the well were not Laban's. He thinks the stone was made large on purpose against anyone minded to foul the water or fill the well up, which is why the first to arrive waited for the rest and they worked in concert, and reports a textual difficulty besides: where the Hebrew says all the flocks were gathered and rolled the stone away, the Samaritan reads shepherds, a reading Houbigant presses hard, since flocks can neither roll a stone nor water sheep. Wesley allows the stone three uses — securing a property in scarce water, saving the well from the sun's heat, and keeping the lambs from drowning in it.

Ellicott rules out one identification, this being not Rebekah's well, which stood just outside the city and was reached by steps, whereas this lies in the open pasture. Rendering the clause as the stone upon the well's mouth was great, he gives the dry country round Haran a practical reason for it — to keep the well from choking with sand — and two social ones, that it restricted the water to fixed hours, needing two or three men to shift it, and that it may have marked private ownership, no possession being more valued than a well. He notices who is served first: the shepherds all wait for Rachel and her sheep drink before flocks that were there long before her, which suggests Laban held at least the first claim, no such courtesy having been shown to the daughters of Jethro. Keil and Delitzsch infer the well's distance from the town from Jacob's having to ask the men where they were from.

debates: What the stone was for. Clarke makes it a guard against tampering that obliged the shepherds to act in concert; Ellicott gives it a practical reason in the sand and two social ones, restricted hours and private ownership; Wesley allows scarcity, the sun's heat, and the safety of the lambs.
themes: the well in the open field
a first claim on the water

schools.summary: Gill observes that Jacob plainly spoke to the keepers and not to the flocks; guesses that Nahor was named rather than Bethuel because Haran was his city, and that Bethuel may have been dead and Laban head of the family; reads the greeting as the Hebrew idiom asking whether there is peace to him, covering health, household and estate together; takes the high day for noon, when flocks in hot countries were made to lie down by still waters; and offers for the refusal either the weight of the stone, which Jarchi says took all the shepherds together, or a custom agreed among them that it should not be opened for any one flock. Calvin hears in the salutation the frankness of that age — the fraternal name is often abused now by dishonest men, but friendly intercourse was then more faithfully cultivated. The same manners explain Rachel's tending the flock, which shows the frugality of a house that abounded with servants and thought it disgraceful to rear children in idleness, softness and indulgence, whereas ambition and refinement have since made manners so effeminate that women are ashamed of their proper office; and they explain the freedom of Jacob's kiss, much greater liberty being allowed in a chaste and modest way of living. Calvin also corrects the order of the narrative: Jacob did not kiss Rachel until he had told her he was her kinsman.

Clarke raises the question how the two parties understood one another, Laban's household speaking Chaldee and not Hebrew, and answers it twice — the names Leah afterwards gave her children show the tongues had many words in common, and Jacob may have learned Chaldee from his mother, whose native speech it was. He glosses the greeting as asking after prosperity, notes that Rachel's name means a ewe and guesses she got it from her fondness for the animals, and reads Jacob's advice as saying that the day is but half run and it is far too early to fold them.

Ellicott makes Nahor the founder of the family, the immigrant from Ur who came to fill Abraham's place when he left. He corrects the phrase about gathering the cattle to folding them, says plainly why Jacob was surprised — several hours of daylight remained — and why the men were not, since if the well was Laban's, waiting for Rachel needed no explanation; and he would render their answer more exactly, then they roll the stone away and we water the sheep, the removal following as soon as all the flocks are collected.

themes: we cannot until all are gathered

schools.summary: Gill puts the kiss after the disclosure, a courtesy once Jacob had told her what she was to him, has the shepherds waiting for that flock alone, and notes with Aben Ezra that the telling came before both the kiss and the weeping.

Henry calls Rachel's keeping the flock her humility and industry, notes that her name signifies a sheep, and says that honest useful labour is what nobody need be ashamed of and no bar to preferment. He reads the meeting as courtship and providence together: knowing his errand, Jacob may well have thought at once that this must be his wife, and being smitten with an honest comely face — sun-burnt, likely, and in the homely dress of a shepherdess — he is wonderfully officious to serve her. That she runs home rather than answer is to her credit, since she would not entertain a kinsman's address without her father's approbation, and such mutual respect at a first interview presaged a happy couple. What looked fortuitous was providence giving Jacob satisfaction the moment he reached the place he was bound for, as Abraham's servant had been met on a like errand. Henry also dismisses the rabbinic conceit that Jacob wept because Eliphaz had waylaid and stripped him at Esau's father's command: it was his passion for Rachel and the surprise of the meeting that drew those tears.

Clarke presses the defence of working women further — they were plainly not shut up at home until marriage, whatever gloss is put on the word for a virgin as one concealed, nor was it beneath the greatest chief's daughters to draw water or herd sheep; wealth then lay in flocks, and honest labour honours high and low alike, there being no discredit in the meanest office that honestly serves the family. He will not let Jacob have all the credit for the stone, Laban's flock being probably the last with a right to the well, so that Jacob assisted the shepherds rather than acting alone. He defends the kiss as the simple and pure way the first inhabitants of the earth testified friendship, abused by hypocrites and disgraced by moralists who stumbled at innocent tokens of kindness while capable of the grossest impurity, and takes the raised voice for thanksgiving and the weeping for a sense of God's goodness and his own unworthiness. Wesley repeats Henry's reading of the meeting almost word for word.

Ellicott brings the scene into his own century, citing Mr Malan's sight of a sheik's daughter driving her fine patriarchal sheep to a well in this very region, and does the arithmetic on Rachel: at least forty years passed between this meeting and the birth of Benjamin, so she must have been a mere child. He gives the same order of events as Gill and makes the sequence the point — Jacob first made himself useful, then said who he was, claimed her as a cousin and kissed her, and only then burst into tears; in that outburst, he says, we see the beginning of his lifelong love for the beautiful child he had so opportunely met.

Gill has the report cover both the kinship and the feat, and notes that the Jewish writers make the message chiefly about the display of strength; he and Clarke gloss the phrase about bone and flesh plainly as nearest kin. Calvin supplies the conversation the narrative omits: Laban had once seen a servant of Abraham's arrive loaded with wealth, so a poor opinion of a nephew who came with nothing might have entered his mind at once, and Jacob had to explain why he had left and why he was so contemptibly clothed — probably with signs and marks his mother had furnished, which is why Laban's exclamation reads as a verdict. Calvin then widens the principle: blood teaches men to help one another, but kindness ought to extend further and diffuse itself through the whole human race, and the spiritual relationship God creates among the faithful ought to be far more effectual still. Of the month he makes a probation, in which Jacob's not sitting idle and eating another's bread for nothing obliged Laban to admit that something beyond his keep was owing; and of Laban's question about serving for nothing he sets out two senses before choosing the second, that Laban was unwilling to exact unpaid service under colour of relationship. What Moses means us to see is a principle of equity in Laban's own mouth — until, a little while after, practice came and Laban forgot every word of it.
Clarke reads son as descendant, Laban being Bethuel's son and Nahor's grandson.

Ellicott explains why the news went to the father rather than the mother's household, as Rebekah's had: this was simply the hospitable reception of a relative, and to Laban it must have been welcome, calling to mind how seventy-seven years before he had watched his sister leave to marry the son of a distant sheik. One thing puzzles him — that so old a man's daughters should be so young — and he offers two solutions, children of a wife of his old age or granddaughters counted as his own, preferring the first since Laban's sons go unmentioned for two chapters. He renders the month exactly as a month of days, meaning a full one.

outliers: Calvin turns Laban's fair-sounding question into a case study in self-deception: men seldom err in general principles and confess with one mouth that every man should have his due, yet the moment they descend to their own affairs self-love blinds them — hence the proverb that nobody is a fit judge in his own cause.
themes: equity in the mouth of Laban

15.pericope_label: The bargain proposed; Leah and Rachel

schools.summary: Gill takes tender-eyed for blear-eyed, a moisture that reddened them and made her less agreeable to look at, though he records that Onkelos rendered it the other way, as if her beauty lay in her eyes and nowhere else.

Henry calls the contract fair and reads Laban's reasoning approvingly — if Jacob is respectful enough to serve for nothing, Laban will not be unjust enough to take advantage of his necessity or his good nature — from which he draws the rule that inferior relations must not be imposed on, and that if it is their duty to serve us it is ours to reward them. He praises what Jacob did with the month, applying himself to his uncle's business like a man of business with no stock of his own, and observes that wherever we are it is good to be employed in something useful. He also does the arithmetic and finds it startling: Jacob was seventy-seven when he bound himself apprentice for a wife and kept sheep for a wife, a thing his posterity are reminded of long afterwards as a mark of the meanness of their origin.

Clarke suspects a motive under Laban's fairness, calling him a very saving if not covetous man who had watched a month's work and meant to secure so useful a servant. On the disputed word he dissents from the others: the Hebrew means soft, delicate, lovely, the reverse of the sense usually given it, and since the writer is comparing the sisters, Leah's chief recommendation was precisely her soft and beautiful eyes while Rachel was beautiful in shape, person, mien and gait. He explains why Jacob offered service rather than money from the custom by which the father received a portion for his daughter rather than giving one with her, quoting a Hindoo lawgiver that a person may become a slave on account of love or to obtain a wife, and turns the point into a complaint about his own age, when the bad education of women makes a dowry necessary, whereas formerly a man who got a wife almost invariably got a prize. Wesley follows Henry, making the age seventy.

Ellicott notes that Jacob had already given a full account of himself on arrival, so Laban probably expected the very answer he got, though the proposal was fair and upright. He agrees with the unflattering sense of the disputed word — Leah, whose name means languor or weariness, had dull bleared eyes, probably from some form of ophthalmia common in that hot sandy region, which in the East counted a great defect where bright eyes were much admired — and ends the comparison where neither of the others goes: it was not Rachel, with her fair face and her husband's lasting love, who became mother of the Messiah's progenitor, but the weary-eyed Leah.

debates: Whether Leah's eyes were a defect or her one beauty. Gill and Ellicott take tender-eyed as blear or dull, a blemish in Eastern reckoning; Clarke argues the Hebrew means soft and lovely and makes her eyes the very thing that recommended her, the comparison still leaving the balance with Rachel; Gill records Onkelos on Clarke's side.

schools.summary: Gill dates the love from the well, Jacob having loved Rachel from the moment he saw her, and will not take Laban's answer at face value, agreeing with the Targum of Jonathan that it was spoken deceitfully by a man who already meant to impose on him. Calvin refuses to call the transaction anything but what it was: a shameful barbarity to hand over a daughter as the reward of service and make her the subject of barter, when Laban should have assigned her a portion and dealt liberally with his son-in-law, and instead defrauded him of his wages under the pretext of kinship. Moses is recording nothing rare, he adds — men do not put their daughters up for sale, but the desire of gain hurries most of them far enough to prostitute their honour and sell their souls. On Jacob's preference Calvin is careful rather than censorious: to be drawn by elegance of form is no sin provided reason keeps the ascendancy, though he suspects self-indulgence in asking the younger sister to the injury of the elder and undervaluing what Leah had. What he praises without qualification is the seven years, in which a man felt no weariness and kept his chastity, living under one roof in daily familiar intercourse and abstaining from every impropriety.

Ellicott attends to how Rachel is named — the Hebrew calls her the little one, as Leah is the great one, meaning simply the younger — and explains the shape of the offer, since wives had to be purchased in the East and Jacob, having brought none of the rich presents Abraham once sent, had nothing but his own service to give. He adds a consequence to watch for: such a sale being ordinarily veiled under the specious form of freewill gifts, both daughters will afterwards be found offended at being so openly bartered. Laban's reply he finds entirely in keeping with the country's custom, Arabs still preferring a relative as husband for a daughter, the elder cousins claiming the elder daughters and the younger the younger, so that Jacob as a second son had a claim upon Rachel; and he reports the rabbinic notion that Leah's eyes were weak from weeping because Esau had never come to marry her, calling it absurd but good evidence that cousin-marriage was an established rule.

debates: Whether Laban's answer was honest. Gill, with the Targum of Jonathan, takes it as spoken deceitfully by a man already meaning to impose on Jacob; Ellicott reads it as the ordinary custom of the country, cousins having a recognised claim on cousins.

schools.summary: Gill says only that Jacob served the whole term, diligently, faithfully and patiently.

Clarke turns the seven years into a survey of how wives were got. In ancient times all nations gave dowries for their wives, and many still do: Shechem offered whatever was asked for Dinah, Eliezer carried a profusion of silver and gold for Rebekah, David had to kill Goliath and then a hundred Philistines for Michal, and Hosea bought his wife for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley; the same held among the ancient Greeks, Indians and Germans, the Romans had a marriage by purchase, and the Tartars and Turks still buy their wives. He then sets down Herodotus on the Babylonians, where every district sold its marriageable virgins once a year, the fairest first and at the highest price, the money from the handsome making the portion of the deformed, with security required of every purchaser that he would live with the woman as his wife — a custom Laban followed in spirit though not in letter when he used Rachel's beauty to dispose of Leah. On the years seeming a few days he reports the opinion that Jacob received Rachel soon after the first month and served afterwards, and the alternative that he was fifty-seven rather than seventy-seven; and he answers the incredulity of the thing twice over, since Jacob had the continual company of his chosen bride and since love affairs among the patriarchs were never carried to the pitch of insanity they reach in modern times. Wesley takes the phrase somewhere else entirely: an age of work will be but a few days to those that love God and long for Christ's appearing.

Ellicott reckons the age at fifty-seven at least and explains it by the late marriages of the patriarchs generally, who arrived at manhood only slowly; on that footing the warmth of Jacob's affection needs no apology, and it was no passing emotion but lasted his whole life. He marks the verse as a turning point, this being the last of the late marriages, since Jacob's own sons married young.

outliers: Clarke's parallel for Laban's dealing is Herodotus on the Babylonian marriage auction, where the price fetched by the beautiful supplied the portion of the deformed — a custom he thinks Laban followed in spirit when he used Rachel's beauty to dispose of Leah.
themes: they seemed but a few days

schools.summary: Gill has Jacob challenge Rachel as his wife already, hers by contract with the conditions performed; takes the feast for a public act, Laban gathering the chief men of Haran to make the marriage open and authentic; sets the substitution after the feast, the guests gone and night fallen, a fit season for such a design; and on the handmaid observes that it was usual to give several at such a time, as Rebekah seems to have had, whereas Leah had one, and that one was the whole portion Jacob got with her — reporting the Targum of Jonathan's claim that Zilpah was Laban's own daughter by a concubine. Calvin restrains the scale of the feast, not a supper for the whole town but many guests as at any splendid wedding, and finds a motive in the splendour: Laban took the more trouble in order to bind Jacob by shame, so that he should not afterwards make light of the marriage he had been tricked into. From the same verse he draws the custom the deception turned on, that out of regard for the modesty of brides they were led veiled into the chamber — that ancient discipline being now thrown off, he adds, men have become almost brutal.

Clarke reads the word for the feast as one of drinking and reasons that sacrifices were probably offered and libations poured out, a cup of wine being handed to every guest with particular ceremonies. He lists the conditions that let the substitution succeed — the bride always veiled, the chamber generally dark, and Leah brought in at evening — and notes the legal point about the handmaid, that slaves given to a daughter at her marriage were her peculiar property, over whom the husband had neither right nor power.

Ellicott glosses the demand as the appointed term of service being finished, and concludes flatly that the marriage took place at the end of the seven years. He adds that the bride was carried closely veiled to the bridegroom's house and that there was probably some similarity of voice and figure between the sisters, then draws a conclusion the others do not: Leah must have been party to the fraud, so that Jacob's later dislike of her was not altogether without reason. On the handmaid he sharpens the comparison, Bethuel having given Rebekah her nurse Deborah and damsels besides, though she had been bought with presents of unusual costliness. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the excuse Laban would make in the morning and refuse it outright: if the custom of not giving the younger before the first-born really held in Haran, as it has in ancient India and elsewhere, he was bound to have told Jacob beforehand.

outliers: Ellicott alone concludes that Leah was a party to her father's fraud, and uses it to make Jacob's later dislike of her not altogether unreasonable.

25.pericope_label: The morning discovery and the excuse

schools.summary: Gill wonders how the night had not betrayed her, unless the sisters sounded alike or Leah kept silence, and finds her hard to excuse — the sin is adultery and incest — though he assembles what can be said: obedience to her father, the wish of an eldest daughter for a husband first, and above all the promised seed that was to run in Jacob's line, with Schmidt's suggestion that Laban had persuaded her the contract was made on her account. He takes Laban at his word about the custom, noting that he denies neither the deceit nor the agreement but pleads the usage of the city against both. Calvin thinks Jacob's expostulation justified and Laban's answer no excuse, though he grants it a pretext, and draws from it the shape of the whole man: once deceitful men have turned aside from truth they make no end of transgressing, and always keep some pretext to clear themselves. He counts the offences in order — seven years' labour demanded for a daughter, the daughter sold without a dowry, and worst of all the nephew robbed of his betrothed wife.

Clarke thinks the rule genuine and old, daughters being early given in marriage by seniority, and remarks that the Hindoos, the oldest people now existing next to the Jews, hold it not as custom but as positive law, counting it an offence equal to adultery to marry while an elder sibling is unmarried — Laban's words, he says, are literally what a Hindoo would say. What he holds against him is the concealment, the custom kept back until Leah had been delivered. Wesley states the retribution in a sentence: Jacob had cheated his own father by pretending to be Esau, and now his father-in-law cheated him; and on the custom he says we have reason to think there was none, and if there was, Laban should have said so when he took seven years' service for the younger daughter.

Ellicott is sceptical of the custom: the practice is such as Laban describes in India, but there is no proof of it among the Bedaween, and since Leah apparently loved Jacob and Laban wanted his service continued, he suspects a plot between the two of them on a pretext overstrained if not false — Jacob plainly knew of no such rule and would never have given seven years for Leah. Keil and Delitzsch look past the excuse to what it produced and refuse both ways of settling it: the bigamy is not to be judged by a Mosaic law against marrying two sisters that did not yet exist, nor set down as incest, as Calvin sets it down, but neither is it justified on the ground that God's blessing afterwards made it the means of multiplying Abraham's seed into a nation.

debates: Whether the custom Laban pleaded existed. Clarke thinks it genuine and ancient, citing Hindoo law, and blames only the concealment; Ellicott finds no evidence of it among the Bedaween and suspects a plot between Laban and Leah; Wesley doubts there was any such custom at all; Gill takes the plea at face value.

schools.summary: Gill takes the week for Leah's, the seven days of marriage feasting and not a week of years of service, citing the Jewish writers and the Targum of Jerusalem. Calvin alone refers the demonstrative to Rachel and reads the verse as the purchase of marriage with her by a second seven years — not that Laban put off the wedding to the term's end, but that Jacob was bound into a fresh servitude. He is harshest of all on Laban, calling him callous in wickedness: had he owned ten more daughters he would have disposed of them the same way, and the graver charge is what he did to the household, involving his nephew in polygamy and setting two sisters in one bed so that each became the other's competitor and they spent their lives in hostility. Better to repudiate an unloved wife, Calvin argues, than keep her captive and let a second consume her with grief — which is why the Lord by Malachi pronounces divorce more tolerable than polygamy. Nor does he let Jacob off: he might have dismissed Leah, who had never been his lawful wife, marriage being constituted by mutual consent, and instead doubled his fault by polygamy and trebled it by an incestuous marriage.

Clarke adds the practical reason Laban could not hand Rachel over at once, the solemnities having begun before all the men of the place, and probably a wish to keep the fraud out of the public eye; he reckons the cost at fourteen years' service instead of seven, since Jacob would hardly have served seven days for Leah, and observes that what a man sows he reaps — Jacob had practised deceit and is now deceived, and Laban was deceived himself after. Wesley reads it as a snare rather than a bargain: Jacob had no design of multiplying wives and would have kept as true to Rachel as his father to Rebekah, having lived without a wife to his eighty-fourth year, and it was Laban who forced him into a strait where he had colourable reason for marrying both.

Ellicott puts the delay in terms of honour, since forsaking Leah during those days would have been an insult her brothers must have avenged, so that Jacob, appeased by the promise of Rachel at the week's end and unwilling to quarrel with the household, submitted to the wrong. He notes that the Hebrew is remarkable — fulfil the week of this, and we will give thee also the this for the service — and insists the idiom means the one and the other, so the first can only be Leah and the second only Rachel.

debates: Whose week the verse means. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott all take it for Leah's marriage feast, Ellicott arguing from the Hebrew idiom that the first demonstrative can only be Leah and the second Rachel; Calvin refers it to Rachel and reads the clause as the purchase of a marriage with her by a further seven years.

28.pericope_label: Rachel given, and seven years more

schools.summary: Gill leaves the justification open. Marrying two sisters was forbidden by the law of Moses and polygamy disallowed later, yet both were dispensed with earlier; he sees an overruling providence, which brings good out of evil, since the Messiah was to spring from Leah and not Rachel, and pleads necessity besides, one sister having been ignorantly defiled and the other his by contract. Calvin takes the whole episode as a warning against the habit of looking to the fathers: Moses meant to exhibit Jacob's sins so that we might learn to fear and square every action by the sole rule of God's word, since if so holy a patriarch fell this grievously, none of us is safe except as God keeps him. It shows how dangerous it is to imitate the fathers while neglecting the law of the Lord — and yet the foolish Papists will observe as law whatever they find the fathers to have done. Nor is Leah spared: she was not despised without fault of her own, having knowingly taken her sister's husband, though her fault is no excuse for Jacob's lust.

Clarke acquits him. It is perfectly plain that Jacob did not serve another seven years before getting Rachel, and such connections, now called incestuous, were allowable then; no blame appears to attach to him, though the women's jealousies vexed him ever after. He even makes the case the origin of a later statute, the law forbidding a man to take a wife to her sister to vex her in her lifetime.

Ellicott asks outright how, after the monogamy of Abraham and the stricter monogamy of Isaac, Jacob came to have two wives, and reports Abravanel's answer that he acted as his brother's substitute in taking the elder and stayed free to marry the younger. His own view is simpler: Jacob regarded Rachel as his own, polygamy was not forbidden, and the only alternative, divorcing Leah, would have been worse. Keil and Delitzsch call it sinful weakness — the fault showing in his loving Rachel more, and the chastisement in the hated wife's being blessed with children while Rachel long remained unfruitful, by which it appeared once more that the origin of Israel was a work not of nature but of grace.

debates: Whether Jacob is to be blamed for the double marriage. Clarke acquits him, the practice being lawful in that age; Ellicott defends him as doing justice to Rachel where divorce would have been worse; Gill leaves it open and pleads necessity and providence; Keil and Delitzsch call it sinful weakness while refusing both Calvin's charge of incest and any justification from the outcome; Calvin holds he doubled his fault by polygamy and trebled it by incest.

schools.summary: Gill takes hated comparatively, since Jacob did a husband's duty to Leah, and lists what may be said for the difference — she had not Rachel's beauty, was never his choice, was imposed on him by deceit. Calvin steers between the extremes and makes the word a charge against Jacob rather than a description of his feelings: Moses chooses so hard a word to amplify the fault of a man who did not discharge a husband's duty. He presses the distinction because many suppose they have done their duty if they stop short of mortal hatred, whereas the Holy Spirit pronounces those hated who are not sufficiently loved — not open displeasure only, but the neglect of brethren and the cold charity that reigns in the world, so that married people who never openly disagree may still be guilty. He also reads the birth as a correction, Jacob's extravagant love being tamed by the rod, and takes from it that offspring is a special gift of God and that children conciliate husbands to wives.

Henry reads the providence as a balancing of accounts: Leah, the less beloved, is blessed with children while Rachel is denied them, Providence keeping the scale even by setting crosses and comforts one against another so that nobody is too much elevated or cast down — Rachel wanting children and having her husband's love, Leah wanting the love and being fruitful, as between Elkana's two wives. The child was three things at once: a rebuke to Jacob for making so great a difference between women he was equally related to, a check to Rachel, and a comfort to Leah under the contempt put on her.

Clarke turns the verse into a rule of interpretation that he thinks settles some disputed passages: to hate, in the idiom, means simply to love less, and on that footing the saying that Jacob was loved and Esau hated means only a greater degree of affection shown to one family than the other, in an earthly portion and in the choice of the Messiah's line — not one word of it touching the eternal state of either nation. Those who prop up the peculiarities of their creed with such texts, he ends, greatly err. Wesley adds the comparison that makes the hard word bearable, that in this sense a man is required to hate father and mother in comparison with Christ.

Ellicott refuses the softening: we must not tone it down too much, for plainly Leah was not the object of love at all; it was her fruitfulness that gave her value in her husband's eyes, and when that ceased he neglected her utterly.

debates: How far to soften the word hated. Gill and Clarke take it comparatively, Clarke building on it a rule that settles the saying about Jacob and Esau; Ellicott refuses the softening and holds Leah was not loved at all; Calvin makes it neither, treating the word as a charge against Jacob for loving insufficiently.

schools.summary: Gill hesitates between two derivations of the first name — see the son, as if she called the household to look, or rather God has seen and provided a son, which he thinks fits the verse better — and allows a guess about her hopes before correcting it: she may have imagined this was the promised seed, but if so she was greatly mistaken, for this son proved unstable and did not excel. He adds that the births came as fast as they well could, and reports the Jewish notion that Leah brought forth her sons at seven months. Calvin makes the naming an act of gratitude and infers a habit of prayer behind it, since thanksgiving is proof of prayer beforehand and those who hope for nothing from God bury his favours in forgetfulness; God's benefits, he adds, were better appreciated in that age than in his own, when a profane stupor so occupies nearly all men that, like cattle, they swallow whatever kindness God bestows. The verse teaches besides that those unjustly despised by men are regarded by the Lord — a consolation to the faithful, who are mostly despised in the world.

Clarke renders the first name literally, behold a son, because Jehovah had looked on her affliction. Wesley reads the series as the record of a marriage: Leah appears very ambitious of her husband's love and reckoned the want of it her affliction, not upbraiding him with it as his fault but laying it to heart as her grief, which she had the more reason to bear because she had consented to the fraud by which she became his wife. Her fourth she called praise — and this, Wesley adds, was he of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came; whatever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving, and all our praises must centre in Christ, as their matter and Mediator both.
Keil and Delitzsch say the names indicate her state of mind throughout, this first taken as a pledge that the Lord had regarded her misery, so that now her husband would love her.

themes: praise and the line of Christ

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the fourth name because of what came out of it: this was a son in whose line and from whose tribe the Messiah was to spring, and Leah, who had praised God already for looking on her affliction and hearing her, now determines to praise him more than ever. He passes on the Targum of Jonathan's reason for the name — that from this son should come kings, and David the king, who should praise the Lord — and asks why she may not as well be supposed to have known that the Messiah would spring from him, which would greatly heighten her joy; and he adds from the Jewish writers a calendar of the four births and the ages the sons reached.

Clarke reads the third name as a calculation, supposing Leah reckoned that after so many children Jacob would be bound to her at least as strongly as to Rachel, and notices where the name led, since from this son sprang the Levites, who instead of the first-born were joined to the priests in the service of the sanctuary. The fourth he renders a confessor, one who acknowledges God and that every good thing comes out of his hand — the name the Jews take from this patriarch, and which, if it could now be rightly applied, would mean a people that confess God. On the closing words he corrects the English: she stood still from bearing is what the Hebrew says, which does not mean she ceased entirely, since she had several children afterwards, the pause being probably caused by a temporary suspension of Jacob's company through Rachel's jealous management.

outliers: Clarke closes the chapter with a complaint about naming in his own day: the ancients called their children after some remarkable providence, whereas we impose names as on cattle, so that the dog, the horse, the monkey and the parrot share names that pass for Christian — some absurd, some ridiculous, and a third sort impious, taken from the demon gods of heathenism.
